To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we discovered a pair of low-mass binaries and measured their masses, which are 0.37 ± 0.05 M_☉ (M_A) and 0.195±0.021 M☉ (M_B) for G78-28 AB, and 0.25±0.06 M☉ ( M_B) and 0.12 ± 0.02 M☉ (MC) for GJ 231.1BC.

(1) we found a pair of M dwarfs orbiting each other with periods of 4.18 yr and 5.4 yr and masses of 0.37 M_☉and 0.195 M_☉; and (2) we found a third M dwarf companion with a period longer than our observing span and masses of 25% of the primary and 12% of the secondary.
we have discovered two new binaries with STEPS and have imaged them with AO, measured their masses, and estimated their spectral types.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the discovery, characterization, and interpretation of low-mass binaries.
the discovery, characterization, and modeling of low-mass binaries, and we present the first results of the STEPS project.
the masses of low-mass stellar and substellar companions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the masses of the components of a binary system can be estimated with an accuracy of ~10%-20%.
the masses are uncertain, with the uncertainties depending on the technique used.
the mass estimates are consistent with the component masses of the components, but the uncertainties are still large.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the mass estimates are in good agreement with the component masses derived from the light ratios and mass-luminosities.
the masses are well determined for G78-28 and poorly determined for GJ 231.
we have found two low-mass binaries, one of which is a triple, and that the masses of these systems are consistent with the masses of field binaries.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the uncertainties on the masses are dominated by the uncertainty on the distance, which is in turn dominated by the uncertainty in the parallax.
the mass of a companion can be constrained by astrometric observations alone if the orbital period is short and the system is bright.
the masses of low-mass companions are more accurately determined by combining astrometric and light ratio data.
